title: Chronic Cranial Window for Imaging Cortical Activity in Head-Fixed Mice
protocol: Prepare the 2–3 months old mouse for surgery.
Weigh the animal.
Induce anesthesia with 3% isoflurane in an induction chamber.
Transfer the mouse to a sterile paper towel.
Inject medetomidine, midazolam, and butorphanol intraperitoneally.
Inject carprofen into the quadriceps muscles.
Inject dexamethasone sodium phosphate into the quadriceps muscles.
Apply ophthalmic ointment to the eyes using small cotton-tips.
Shave the head with a veterinary hair clipper designed for small animals.
Apply hair-removal cream over the shaved scalp.
Clean off the hair-removal cream after 5 minutes using small cotton-tips.
Wash residual hair-removal cream and disinfect the area with iodine or 70% ethanol.
Fixate the head in a stereotaxic frame using blunt ear bars.
Wipe the scalp with cotton swabs soaked in iodine.
Apply Lidocaine topically for local anesthesia using a cotton swab.
Wait 3-5 min for induction of local anesthesia.
Glue headplate with dental acrylic.
Make a midline incision above the skull from just behind the eyes to the posterior end of the skull.
Remove scalp skin on both sides of the incision, ensuring only hairless areas are cut.
Push remaining skin to the side using Lidocaine-soaked cotton-tips.
Scrape connective tissue and muscles away from lateral and posterior bone ridges using tweezers.
Level the skull along the midline axis at the suture intersection points bregma and lambda.
Use a reference pipette fixed on a micromanipulator orthogonally to ensure alignment.
Lower the pipette onto bregma and zero the coordinates.
Locate the center of the future cranial window over V1: 3.5 mm posterior and 2.4 mm lateral from bregma.
Go up with the pipette and mark the location below the pipette with a fine-tip water-resistant marker.
Mark anterior, lateral, and medial points 1.5 mm and posterior point about 3 mm from the center.
Ensure that all coordinates are adapted for different target regions.
Critical: Mark the posterior position behind the transverse sinus to avoid damage during craniotomy.
Move the pipette out of the workspace without changing the bregma zero coordinates.
Engrave the skull bone with a circle connecting the marked points around the center point using the dental drill with a 0.5 mm diameter drill bit.
Do not drill deep; this groove is only for marking the future craniotomy.
Thin the bone around the engraving with a 1- or 1.2-mm diameter drill bit at a speed of 3×104 rpm.
Stop thinning when tiny cracks appear around the engraving.
Stop thinning if the bone inside the engraving can be easily pushed with gentle force from tweezers.
Drill carefully, with smooth motion, keeping the drill at a shallow angle and applying minimal pressure with the drill bit.
Periodically cool and clean the bone with saline during drilling.
Spray the area gently with compressed air to maintain cleanliness.
Use a small cotton-tip or flat-tip forceps in the contralateral hand for better control during drilling.
Glue a wooden stick vertically to the center of the craniotomy bone using gel superglue.
Press the glued stick slightly against the bone for 10–15 seconds and let it set for 5 minutes.
Use a stick with a diameter slightly smaller than the craniotomy bone.
Gently lift and tilt the stick backward to separate the attached bone patch from the dura while pressing the anterior part of the skull downwards with a cotton swab or the flat side of the tweezers.
If cracks are visible, use fine-tip tweezers when lifting the stick.
Pulling the bone up will minimize the risk of dura damage and help to cut-open the skull.
If no cracks appear, or appear when lifting, remove the stick by scraping the glue from the bone using tweezers.
Proceed with more thinning of the bone around the engraving.
Be prepared to use a sterile sponge moisturized with saline or Carprofen if bleeding occurs.
Clean the dura with gel-foam sponge moistened with saline or Carprofen.
Add a drop of saline to the dry dura to check for bleeding.
Glue the cranial window only after ensuring no damaged blood vessels are present and there is no bleeding.
Inject retrogradely transported fluorescent beads into the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN).
Inject viral vector AAV1.hSyn.TurboRFP.WPRE.rBG into the dLGN.
Return the reference pipette to the zeroed bregma coordinates.
Record the difference in ventral direction between 0 and the bone surface if the bone was thinned over the bregma point.
Remove the reference pipette.
Connect the silicone tubing to the end of the injection pipette and fix it in the holder.
Select a pipette with short shaft for injections into the upper cortex.
Use a pipette with long shaft for deep cortex (layers 5 or 6) or sub-cortical areas to minimize tissue damage during insertion.
Carefully lower the pipette tip onto the bone of the bregma.
Zero the coordinates.
Lift the pipette up the recorded distance from 0 in step 16a.
Zero the coordinates again.
Tip-fill the pipette with a tracer containing solution.
Cut a 5×10 mm piece of parafilm with the protective wax paper attached.
Mix a 2 μL drop of tracer solution (mixed 1:1 with PBS and sonicated for 5–10 s) with 2 μL drop of AAV solution on the parafilm.
Remove the protective wax paper.
Place the parafilm on the ear-bar within the working distance of the micromanipulator.
Apply weak positive pressure (10–14 hPa) and lower the pipette tip into the drop under visual guidance.
Tip-fill the pipette with up to 300 nL of solution using negative pressure (typically −150 to −200 hPa).
Replace the pipette in case of clogging; remove the clogged pipette and try a larger tip diameter pipette or additional dilution with PBS.
Apply weak positive pressure (10–14 hPa) and lift the pipette up.
Maintain this pressure until the injection of the solution into the brain.
Maintain positive pressure to counteract capillary effects and prevent air or cerebrospinal fluid from entering the pipette.
Wipe the pipette tip with a PBS-soaked sterile sponge.
Inject the tracer solution smoothly into the brain using bregma as the origin of the coordinate system.
Position the pipette at 2.45 mm posterior, 2.4 mm lateral, and 2.9 mm ventral for dLGN targeting.
Wait for 3–5 minutes at the target location to allow tissue sealing around the pipette wall before injection.
Under visual observation, inject approximately 150–200 nL of the prepared solution into the tissue using positive pressure (35-70 hPa).
Reduce positive pressure to 10-14 hPa and wait for 10 minutes to allow the injected solution to spread into the tissue.
Slowly and smoothly retract the pipette after injection.
Tilt the head of the mouse by 5°–10° in the horizontal plane to level the edges of the craniotomy on the latero-medial axis.
Clean the coverslip with alcohol and compressed air.
Place the coverslip on the dura.
Slightly press the coverslip with a small cotton-tip so that it attaches to the dura on a large area of the craniotomy.
Add a drop of saline onto the center of the craniotomy if the brain surface appears concave due to low blood pressure or deep anesthesia.
Keep the dura intact throughout the surgery.
Avoid attempts to remove the dura to prevent bleeding and brain damage.
Use hydroperoxide to separate the dura from the pia mater if removal is necessary.
Open the separated dura carefully using fine-tip forceps.
Glue the coverslip by applying small drops of liquid superglue to the edges of the glass.
Press the coverslip in the center with a small cotton-tip to prevent glue spread under the glass.
Pick up droplets of regular superglue with a narrow but flat end wooden stick from parafilm.
Add extra drops of glue around the window coverslip without pressure from above to ensure complete sealing.
Glue can be added directly on the dura if the craniotomy area is not fully covered by the coverslip.
Position the aluminum headplate over the coverslip parallel to the eye-line.
Mount the headplate at approximately the same level as the glass coverslip.
Ensure that the headplate and coverslip planes are parallel.
Place the cut edge of the central hole on the upper side.
Attach the headplate to the skull with a small drop of superglue.
Prepare dental acrylic according to the producer's instructions.
Glue the headplate to the skull by filling all spaces under and around the headplate, including edges of the glass window and exposed skull.
Pick up droplets of dental acrylic with a narrow but flat end wooden stick.
Cover all exposed bone with dental acrylic to prevent infection.
Continue filling dental acrylic under the headplate while holding the mouse.
Ensure strong fixation of the headplate with dental acrylic to cover a large area of bone.
Add temporally 0.5%–1% isoflurane anesthesia if the mouse shows reflexes or reactions during surgery.
Inject saline (10–20 μL/g, s.c.) every hour during surgery to avoid dehydration.
If medetomidine was used for anesthesia, inject Atipamezole hydrochloride (0.3 μL/g, i.p.) after surgery for faster waking.
Prior to the mouse waking up, inject analgesic (Buprenorphine dissolved in 0.9% saline; 0.1 μg/g, s.c.) to ease pain and distress.
Add recovery food supplement (DietGel 76a, Clearh2o) to the cage post-surgery.
Check the mouse regularly for signs of pain and omission of grooming following surgery.
Inject analgesic (Buprenorphine 0.1 μg/g, s.c.) if the mouse shows signs of pain after surgery.
If the brain shows signs of inflammation or blood under the window following surgery, inject immunosuppressant (e.g., Carprofen 10 μg/g body weight, i.p.) for 2–3 consecutive days.
